title: Ohio Travel Forecast Performance
text:
Traffic forecast accuracy has long been a source of uncertainty in transportation planning and research. While travel forecasting is subject to numerous factors that might impact accuracy — the volume of expected traffic, rural-urban location, availability of data, etc. — trends remain understudied, and insufficiently understood.





“… projections of future traffic conditions on existing or proposed roadways. Traffic forecasts are used to inform important decisions about transportation projects, including the selection of which projects to build and certain design elements of those projects.”
— NCHRP Report 934, 2020, p. 5-1


Lack of data is commonly offered as a reason for the historical lack of research into forecast accuracy, and for good reason. Before automated advances in count technology, collecting accurate data on roadway traffic was laborious, involving manual counts of cars passing along a stretch of roadway. This limiting the ability of forecasters to check their work after the fact.
Fortunately, these constraints are a thing of the past, but standards and best practices for accuracy assessment remain limited. As noted in NCHRP Report 934, the process for assembling these data requires considerable labor by digging through old (and often un-digitized) forecasting documents, sourcing forecast-year traffic data for road segments, and subsequently pairing segment-level forecasts to appropriate data.


My work on this subject involved all elements of the process described above — including advancing the methodologies and tools to manage data once assembled. Unlike other aspects of traffic engineering, no standard software is used for this process, as data availability, formatting, and forecasting methods vary state-by-state.
For this work in the Ohio Department of Transportation’s Modeling and Forecasting section, I developed custom scripts in R to facilitate the processing, analysis, and visualization of ODOT’s travel forecasting data. This work resulted in the 2025 Forecast Accuracy Assessment and technical report, which was the state’s first such report completed in eleven years.

title: Modeling Green Infrastructure Co-Benefits
text:
As a major city of the Great Lakes region, and sitting at the confluence of three major rivers, flooding has long threatened Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Following major floods in 1997 and 1998, the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District (MMSD) began vigorously expanding its use of green infrastructure (GI) across the Milwaukee metro area. Through trees, bioswales, green roofs, and other forms of GI, this strategy aims to mitigate urban flooding by increasing low-cost storage capacity. GI holds water where it falls, thus reducing stress on the sewer network during storms.






Figure 1: MMSD GI by Year













“… an approach to wet weather management that is cost effective, sustainable, and environmentally friendly. Green infrastructure management approaches and technologies infiltrate, evapotranspire, capture, and reuse stormwater to maintain or restore natural hydrology.”
— US EPA, 2010, p. 31




Proponents of GI commonly tout its claimed co-benefit effects — the positive, ancillary impacts of these technologies beyond their core function in wet weather management. The MMSD has long argued for GI on the basis of co-benefits, such as increasing nearby property values, air and water quality improvements, reducing urban heat island effects, and reducing crime in the surrounding area.
Reduced incidence of crime around GI may occur for many reasons. Evidence and theory suggests that planted greenery may indicate maintenance, leading to greater surveilance of criminal activity in an area. Moreover, studies have shown that planted greenery reduces physiological and mental markers of stress, which could reduce the incidence of crime. Alternatively, GI has increasingly been linked to “green gentrification”, which suggests that the socioeconomic conditions of greened neighborhoods may change, leading to fewer drivers of crime.

title: Modeling Green Infrastructure Co-Benefits
text:
Research
My research centered on the evaluation of claimed reductions to the incidence of crime, asking three questions:

Q1) Is there a relationship between the MMSD’s construction of GI and changes in neighborhood-level criminal activity in the City of Milwaukee, Wisconsin?
Q2) If GI is associated with lower crime, are its effects sustained or temporary?
Q3) What kinds of crime are most impacted — if any — by the installation of GI? Are effects uniform, or do they vary based on the offense?


Methods
My research relied on a staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) design – also known as an event study or stacked DiD — in order to examine the effect of green infrastructure on crime. The MMSD installed GI in different places at different times, and this staggered deployment challenges a traditional DiD research method that asks: “What effect followed from an intervention, relative to what came before it?”
By constructing a panel dataset with treatment year cohorts, as shown in the flowchart below, my research controlled for the year that GI was installed in a location. This allowed me to compare like with like when assessing the incidence of crime; criminality in a newly-treated census tract shouldn’t be compared to criminality in a tract that was treated two years prior. Rather, tracts are only compared to those which are also being newly treated with GI or those which have not yet received GI. This allows a reliable, controlled assessment of what effect GI actually had on neighborhood crime.
With this data in hand, I used fixed effects Poisson regressions to assess the relationship between GI installation and local incidence of crime.



Figure 2: Research Design: Staggered (“Stacked”) Difference-in-Differences

title: Modeling Green Infrastructure Co-Benefits
text:
Findings
My work did find evidence that the incidence of specific crimes falls following the installation of GI, but with a few caveats.
First, some crimes become less likely, though not all are impacted. Opportunistic and property-based crimes — vehicle break-ins, vehicle thefts, larceny, and burglary — fall modestly in an area following GI installation. Additionally, violent assaults seem to fall around newly-installed GI, which may include both premeditated violence and spur-of-the-moment assaults. Conversely, other violent crimes — homicide, sex offenses, and robbery — are unimpacted by GI.
Second, some effects last longer than others. Opportunistic crimes show the most promising reductions, with evidence that the co-benefit effect is sustained for at least 2-3 years post-installation. Assessing property crimes alone reveals a more narrow effect window, with crime falling in the installation year, followed by a rebound to normal conditions.
Third, reductions to crime are modest (3-7% annually), though the cumulative effect of these interventions is meaningful over time. There is no silver bullet that can stop crime from occurring, but the effect of many interventions can help communities thrive.
This evidence suggests that the MMSD’s GI policy does offer claimed co-benefit effects, providing social benefits to Milwaukee communities.

title: Lima, OH Site Redevelopment
text:
The City of Lima, Ohio faces challenges common to many Rustbelt cities: an aging population, loss of its industrial base, and the need for economic revitalization. This proposal examines one of many sites for potential redevelopment in Lima, situated directly southeast of downtown Lima at the intersection of Elm and Metcalf Streets, from which the site takes its name.
In this project for a graduate course on site planning, my team reimagined the Elm + Metcalf site in phases. Starting with removing vacant structures and introducing local programming, redevelopment moves to the construction of a new business venue and expanded green space. The final proposal better situates the site in its surrounding neighborhood.

title: Lima, OH Site Redevelopment
text:
Site & Land Use
Elm + Metcalf is located in a low-density neighborhood of mixed commercial and residential development. As Lima’s zoning is cumulative, housing intermingles considerably with local business – zoning does not perfectly reflect parcels’ land uses.
The site is roughly divided into four quadrants. A Habitat For Humanity ReStore and its two large parking lots occupy three quarters of the site. The last section – in the northwest corner – hosts the Lima Adult Learning Center and a vacant corner parcel with two dilapidated structures. This section lies atop a high retaining wall that internally divides the site.

title: Lima, OH Site Redevelopment
text:
Design Challenges
Topography presents the single greatest challenge to coherent site design. The retaining wall rises to more than eight feet high, severely limiting movement between except around the site’s periphery. Given the integration of uses called for in our proposal, our design includes a new stairway in the center of the site.
Parking issues can be abated by greater movement from the top and bottom of Elm + Metcalf. Two large parking lots take up significant space on-site, yet these are underused in off-peak business hours. Given the limited space for redevelopment in the northwest corner, our proposal includes a shared parking agreement between Elm + Metcalf’s three land owners.
Hydrology poses yet another challenge to site design. Evidence of ponding can be found across the site, with topography as the main culprit. Water flows inward from Metcalf into the southwest parking lot, and this is only partially captured by an internal storm drain. The northern parking lot and northwest corner also show evidence of ponding, which was reflected in the results of a hydric flow model run in the course of our analysis.
With redevelopment potential concentrated on the northwest corner, design choices revolve around how a new, vibrant use impacts the site, and how the coordinated uses can work better than disperate ones do presently.

title: Lima, OH Site Redevelopment
text:
Proposal
Our proposal responded to these challenges and was based on the following design aims:



Reactivate the Northwest Parcels  — Encourage development along a busy corridor  — Remove blighted structures; potential USTs 
Expand Community & Green Space  — A new gathering space for Lima residents  — Beautify the area and reduce impervious surface
Improve Stormwater Management  — Identify sites of ponding and poor flow  — Incorporate green infrastructure where suitable

Plan Phased Development  — Realistic development timelines  — Exploring how to better coordinate land uses
Unify the Site & Area Identity  — Leverage site assets to improve the whole  — Reimagine Elm + Metcalf in the community
Coordinate Parking  —  Reduce total parking on-site, especially NE lot  —  Make more efficient use of existing parking

title: Ithaca, NY Green Space Inventory
text:
Ithaca is a small city of 30,000 residents in New York’s Finger Lakes region. The city possesses significant natural assets, a robust parks portfolio, and hosts major institutions like Cornell University.
In 2018, the City of Ithaca adopted its current Parks and Recreation Master Plan to inventory local assets, guide future projects, and structure decision-makers’ thinking around supply, demand, and access to facilities. However, this work contains notable omissions relevant to the planning process; green space and riverine gorges located maintained by Cornell University, while obliquely considered in the report, does not feature centrally in the City’s inventory. Similarly, the surrounding region contains extensive trails, green space, and recreational facilities that are accessible to the local population, yet absent from the City’s report. These omissions have consequences for the planning process and the public’s understanding of local conditions.
My work is both more targeted and of a larger scope than the 2018 Master Plan. It looks more specifically at residents’ access to existing parks and recreational facilities, but it also includes locations omitted from the Master Plan.
At its core, my work asks the following questions: Who has access to Ithaca’s park facilities, in what places, and to what kinds of amenities?



Figure 1: Topographic Map of Ithaca area with green spaces

title: Michael Vargo
text:
Bio
I’m an urban planner, GIS specialist, and data researcher with experience in transportation planning (particularly for transit and active mobility), sustainability initiatives for municipal land use, and data-driven policy evaluation.
I am currently seeking full-time work in private- or public-sector planning, data analytics, or geospatial analysis, having recently completed my Master of City and Regional Planning from The Ohio State University (2024-2026). Read more About Me or see my Portfolio for more information.
Feel free to contact me regarding career opportunities with your organization. I am open to work anywhere in the US or Canada, with preferences for locations in the Great Lakes or Pacific Northwest.

title: About Michael Vargo
text:
Michael Vargo is an urban planner, GIS specialist, and data researcher based in Columbus, Ohio.
He has worked at Ohio Department of Transportation in the Division of Planning, where he authored the state’s first comprehensive report on travel forecast accuracy assessment in over a decade. Findings from this assessment, along with technical materials created in support of the work, provide ODOT with a clearer understanding of trends in forecast error. This work dovetailed with research from the Federal Highway Administration into nationwide forecast accuracy, through which he collaborated with contracted research teams on the design and performance of tools for forecast accuracy assessment.
Prior to planning, Michael worked as a high school English language instructor in rural eastern France. He also served as a teaching assistant for a mixed graduate and undergraduate course on transportation and land use during grad school. He greatly enjoys all elements of the teaching process, whether leading instruction, designing coursework, or advising students.
Michael attended the Ohio State University for his Master of City and Regional Planning, along with his Bachelor of Arts in Arabic, French, and Political Science. He also studied at Middlebury Language Schools’ Arabic program.

Research & Interests






Urban Policy

Public housing policy and its market impacts 
Transit-oriented development 
Urban economics and econometric methods 
Densification and urban revitalization 
Access to urban green space 
Open-source data






Transportation

Active mobility policy and infrastructure planning 
Transit systems and micromobility integration 
Planning, use, and expansion of greenways 






Language & Culture

Arab and Iranian Sufi literature 
Links between Sufi and Catholic mystic traditions 
Calligraphic traditions of the Mediterranean 
The works of Simone Weil
Anglophone Irish poetry 
The art of Maria Helena Vieira da Silva 
Foreign language acquisition and education






Personal
Michael is originally from Columbiana, Ohio, where he grew up on a maple syrup and Christmas tree farm. A fan of the outdoors, he enjoys birding, biking, hiking, and bouldering, and can often be found biking along one of Central Ohio’s many trails.
Michael also loves good espresso, making fun maps, and reading books in new languages (currently Portuguese). Floral button downs, German pop music, and reading the latest edition of The Economist bring him joy.
